item.content:encoded:
Álvaro Lozano-Robledo, Professor of Mathematics at the University of Connecticut and on Youtube

In reply to Who will become the new mathematicians of Math 2.0? by Anonymous

SERIES · As application deadlines approach, Proofs and Prompts is publishing a series of posts from 19 to 23 October for people considering a PhD, doing a PhD or looking for a postdoc: guidelines, discussions and speculation about what to do and what careers in mathematics will look like. This post is one of them. Each is written independently and reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

This is a response to a recent post on Proofs and Prompts titled “Who will become the new mathematicians of Math 2.0?” written by an Anonymous PhD student (who I will refer to as “Anonymous” below). I would urge particularly all tenured and tenure-track mathematicians to read it because there are many students that think the same way, and are planning to leave academia as a consequence.

I recently wrote a guest piece on Terry Tao’s blog (“What should we tell our students?”) where I warned that we are ‘about to lose an entire generation of mathematicians’ so I feel a duty to reply to Anonymous’ post, to try to offer some counterpoints to the arguments expressed therein. More importantly, I feel a duty to talk to my students about these issues, and I have shared Anonymous’ post with them, so that we can have a discussion. I hope my colleagues in the mathematical community reach out to their students as well.

In order to respond to Anonymous, I will quote some key sentences, and then elaborate with my own thoughts.

I recently heard a mathematician say that it is “paradoxical” to not want to study a field that is undergoing a scientific revolution in reference to October 6th. This mindset completely misses the point of why I do mathematics, and I suspect this is true for many other graduate students and even other established mathematicians.

I want to start here because I believe I may be one of the mathematicians that they are referring to. In a video discussing my post on Tao’s blog, I said

“And I think it would be in fact paradoxical that people would not want to join a field of study during a scientific revolution where we’re seeing this incredible acceleration.”

I will come back to the ‘paradoxical’ remark later on, but I want to first mention what I said right after that quote:

“It is somewhat chaotic. It seems somewhat confusing to be a mathematician right now. But we are trying to figure out together what should the math landscape look like in a year and in five years and how to navigate… how we can use LLMs in ethical ways and in a way that is going to construct solid mathematics along the way and in a way that the mathematical field is going to thrive.”

Let me elaborate on that. Historic upheavals of the status quo are usually chaotic while they happen, and in many cases many of those living through such times have been trampled and mistreated (with such dramatic and relevant examples as the industrial revolution). It is the duty of those in positions of power or security to fight for the rights and well-being of those who may be more likely to suffer through a revolution. In our case, we are living through what can be considered a technological revolution that has great potential to accelerate research and progress and, at the same time, it has a terrifying civilization-ending non-zero potential. Unfortunately, trying to pretend that the revolution is not happening, or trying to preserve the status quo, only delays the inevitable, and prevents communities from fully preparing and reinforcing their core values, so that their professions can survive said revolution.

If we limit our conversation to mathematics and the mathematical community, the LLMs have already revolutionized research mathematics, with the proposed resolution of several landmark conjectures, such as Navier-Stokes or the quasi Riemann hypothesis. This is undeniable and, simply put, we must learn how to coexist with this new technology. But they are also an existential threat to the way mathematics works, and the way the mathematical community operates. So it is absolutely normal and expected to be excited about the research advances, and also extremely concerned about the ways it may change our field, as Anonymous very eloquently points out.

In particular, while the OAI drop of October 6th is certainly of “historic” proportions, it clearly also has had a disruptive effect of historic proportions. Whether the global effect of the LLMs will be a net positive will be determined much later in the future. But it is clear that the “arms race” of frontier model companies to develop ever more capable mathematical models is a corporate publicity stunt and, very early on, even before the Fields medalists warned of a misalignment in an open letter, I asked mathematicians not to be complicit in such an arms race.

At the end of my video about the Oct 6 drop, I encouraged people to stay in the field to make changes from within the community. It is up to us in the profession, and more so up to the newer generations, to lead the way to ethical and sustainable research practices that will allow mathematics to prosper. How to do so is to be decided, so all of Anonymous points are well taken. Whatever we do, we need to make sure students do not abandon mathematics because they think it has become unrecognizable. But the key question is: who is in charge of making these changes and laying out a path forward? I claim that no one is in charge, and we all are. Precisely those that see the field driving towards a cliff, have a great role to play within the community to warn about such dangers! It is a chaotic time, the future is uncertain, and this is disconcerting, but I think there are many reasons to be optimistic and to continue in the mathematical profession.

Now let me backtrack in Anonymous’ post to the very first line:

To the mathematicians shaping the future of our profession,

The mathematical community is not monolithic, and this is a feature, not a bug, of the community. There is no single person, group, or entity that dictates what mathematicians do or how they should operate. In particular, Terry Tao is not a spokesperson for all of mathematics and, of course, there are many out there that do not agree with his views and his predictions for the future of mathematics. Personally, I highly value and respect many of the things he has said, and I disagree with others. I single out Tao here because Anonymous does, but we could similarly agree or disagree on Tsimerman’s or Duminil-Copin’s points… or any other non-Fields medalist point of view, from one of the many recent blog posts on the matter of AI.

Right now, there are many different groups trying to pull mathematics in very different directions. For example, while some mathematicians are completely embracing LLMs, other mathematicians completely refuse to use LLMs in their work. Some of us are choosing the middle ground, and we use LLMs with caution for certain tasks, we avoid them for other more intellectual tasks, while respecting the decisions of some of our colleagues (I include students in this category) who cherish them, or do not wish to use them at all.

When students choose graduate programs, and PhD advisors, many of us encourage them to ask lots of questions (to the staff, to faculty members, to students, to friends) about the atmosphere in the department, and their practices, and about the personalities of the potential advisors. Similarly, I would encourage students who are thinking of a career in mathematics to reach out to their current or prospective programs and advisors, and enquire about their stance on AI/LLM use. Does it match the student’s own attitude towards AI, or is it antithetical to their ideals? Since the community is far from monolithic, there are plenty of departments and potential advisors that will be aligned with whatever views the student holds, and it would be wise to choose programs based on that type of alignment, if the issue of AI is key in the decision making.

I love technical work. I love spending days, weeks, months working on a lemma or an idea without success. […] As AI has now become highly capable of performing this kind of work, I see shockingly little from the mathematics community about how this kind of crisis in education will be addressed.

There was a recent summit on “PhD Math Education in the Age of AI” and the recommendations for graduate programs can be found here. TPSE is putting together a panel discussion on the Future of Graduate Education in Mathematics. Many departments are having internal discussions on how to approach these issues. As I said above, the future is uncertain but we are trying to think of the best possibilities in education as well as in research.

What is the goal of a graduate program in mathematics? How do we define success in a PhD program? In my opinion, the PhD is an apprenticeship, and success is measured by whether the candidate has been trained and is proficient in all aspects of the mathematical profession. At the end of their degree, several mathematicians write letters of recommendation. A (good) rec letter or set of letters evaluates the PhD candidate’s aptitude in all of these aspects: research potential, teaching abilities, service to the community, potential as a colleague, etc. And then colleagues in other institutions read these letters and determine whether the candidate will be a good match for the research and/or teaching needs of their department. Many of the conversations surrounding AI concentrate on the research aspects, but there is a lot more to being a mathematician than just research.

On the subject of research aptitude, will letters in the future refer to the fantastic LLM skills of the candidate? Will we compare students and say such and such student is in the top 2% of LLM-prompters that we have ever met? Will we say wonderful things about their slop-paper output in our letters? Will we praise the many slop-papers that they have been able to de-slopify? I do not think so – we will still need to have a way to measure their research potential based on their own capability of thinking deeply about problems, and coming up with innovative ways to attack interesting problems. It is absolutely true, as Anonymous points out, that students need to spend long hours thinking deeply about a problem, and I do not think LLMs should change that. So PhD advisors should encourage students not to use LLMs for certain tasks such as proof generation of key lemmas, because these are the tasks where intellectual development actually happens (see the Specific Recommendations in the section on Research and AI in the recommendations from the Summit). In a recent conference I was at, someone suggested to grad students to always be working on at least one project that is completely LLM-free.

As a result, I do not think anyone should or will rob the students from their long hours working on a lemma by “pure thought” because most of us recognize the irreplaceable value of the time spent on that activity. It is precisely the outcome of those thinking sessions that sets students apart at the time of evaluating their intellectual and research ability in research letters.

On the other hand, if an advisor demands results with a quick turnaround, and expects that the student will access an LLM for help to be able to move on – against the wishes of the student – then it is time to choose a different advisor. The ideal scenario is that the student will ask the advisor for help or a hint on how to proceed, even if an LLM could provide such ideas, because those conversations are actually also part of the apprenticeship: students learn how to collaborate with other mathematicians through those interactions. Plus the advisor may have a much better intuition than the LLM does anyway.

Many celebrate the possibility that AI will relieve them of the burden of difficult calculations, technical lemmas, and other supposedly tedious aspects of mathematical research.

I do not think that is a common sentiment. For the most part, we all value the time spent in understanding the technical difficulties of key lemmas. On the other hand, LLMs can be fantastic tools in helping us write code and run numerical experiments. I am not great at coding, and I find that the LLMs are allowing me to run computations that I only dreamed possible. It would have been very tedious for me to learn how to write code in Python, html, javascript, etc., but now I am able to create code in all those languages, run experiments, and later verify the results mathematically, all in hours instead of weeks (or instead of never!).

Terence Tao has proposed a vision of a new way of doing mathematics, Math 2.0, where the emphasis moves away from solving open problems and toward a more holistic approach. […] But I feel like I am asking the obvious question that has not been addressed: What if I do not want to spend my professional life doing these activities?

Two points here. One (1), some of us have always had a holistic approach to a PhD: I have always emphasized to my students that I expect them to become well-rounded mathematicians, not just great researchers, and that means that I try to push them not just to write a great thesis, but to be better instructors, better members of the community, better at networking, better colleagues, better at giving talks at all levels, etc. There is nothing wrong with a holistic approach, and in fact it makes candidates more appealing to a broader range of colleges and universities at the time of applying for jobs.

And two (2), many do not agree with Tao’s vision either, and that is ok. In my research, I want to solve problems. The coolest the problem the better. I do want to think about a problem and come up with an ingenious solution, and then tell the world about it. I do not want to inherit a slop-solution to a problem that a company dropped in a repository, and try to make sense of it. I would not want to do that, and I would not expect a student to want to do that either, so I would not ask a student to do that as part of their duties to complete a PhD. I simply do not think we will move in the direction of “moving away from solving problems.”

However, I have thought of problems that an LLM could solve, prompted them, and now I have LLM-prepared drafts on problems I care about. Instead of posting these papers directly to Hexagonmath.org, say, my current strategy is to introduce students to research by explaining the problem I am interested in, explaining why others are also interested in the same problem, discussing the idea that led me to prompt an LLM, and sharing the paper with the student. Then use that paper and that topic as a thread for an independent study on the particular area, so that the student learns enough background to understand the motivation for the paper, and the techniques that are used to solve the problem. Later, we will read together the LLM draft, understand the proof, and rewrite it in a way we understand and can make sense of it. While we think about the proofs, I hope we come up with ways to extend the arguments to strengthen the result, or apply the techniques to other similar problems. And finally polish the paper so that we can submit it to a journal, so that the student has an early experience in writing a research paper, and so that they have published a paper early on to talk about during research conferences. A paper they understand and they can feel is their own, because they have contributed to make it their own.

Will this strategy work? I do not know! I am just trying things out, honestly, and I am listening to any other mathematicians who are trying out different strategies to coexist with the new technology.

I do not expect to follow this early-LLM-draft protocol for a thesis problem, however. It would only be appropriate just as some first steps into research.

There is a problem with the proposed future of mathematics, and it is more concerning than my personal dissatisfaction. How exactly do you expect to train the next generation of mathematicians? You know how to formulate new research directions. Where did these skills come from? I doubt they were developed by reading successful proofs or listening to an explanation of an idea.

As a matter of fact, I do not think intuition and mathematical taste is learned by thinking deeply about a problem for hours on end. I have learned much more attending lectures and conferences, and talking to other mathematicians during lunches and dinners. I have had my best ideas reading other people’s papers and proofs. As an anecdote, early on in my career I signed up to write brief reviews for MathSciNet. I am not sure exactly why, but I was assigned to read and review several articles by Bo-Hae Im (some solo papers, and some co-authored by Im and others), and after reading the third or fourth paper by Im dealing with a conjecture of Larsen, I had an idea of how to prove a related result. I wrote to Im and we ended up collaborating on a research article that eventually was published by the Journal of the London Mathematical Society (and it had a significant impact in getting tenure).

As I mentioned above, we should make an explicit effort to allow students to think deeply about problems, but we should also make it clear that students should be reading papers and proofs. And whether we like it or not, some of the proofs dropped by OAI contain some interesting arguments that we should absolutely study and think about! A particularly valuable example is the proof of the non-existence of Siegel zeros, which several mathematicians (Banks, Kerr, Green, Barreto) have improved on, and now it seems the papers have converged to a remarkably simple argument that many of us would highly benefit from understanding.

Back to the question on how to train the next generation of mathematicians… I am not sure we have the answers yet, but I do not think it will look dramatically different from what we do now. There is a new tool in town, yes, but the guiding principles should be the same: train students to be well-rounded mathematicians.

If the future consists of interpreting AI generated results, organizing knowledge, and directing automated research, why should I remain in academia?

The way this question is phrased, it assumes that the worst, most dystopian possible scenario will come to pass, where AI can solve any single problem humans could solve, and that we would reach a point where only machines do math research. As I mentioned in my piece in Tao’s blog, the future of LLM capabilities is completely unclear. There are many ways in which LLMs could hit a limit in mathematics, for example from the theoretical or feasibility points of view. The frontier model companies are driving the narrative and trying to convince us all that their products are already super human when this is far from the truth. I wish mathematicians had a multi-million PR team behind them to build praise and support for our fantastic research record!

The reality is that many of us have started using LLMs to aid our research, as a tool or as a collaborator, and it turns out that it can be very exciting and fulfilling to do so. As one of the best recent examples of LLM use I know of, one of my colleagues (Kyu-Hwan Lee) joined a team of mathematicians to prove that the sporadic simple group M_23 is Galois over Q. Their team succeeded with the help of LLMs in a task that many had tried and failed, and made some really interesting progress in the inverse Galois problem. Here is an excerpt from their declaration of AI use:

“No text in this article was written by AI. Our work relies on longstanding domain knowledge and techniques for computing curves of positive genus [KMSV14]. The key strategic decisions and the conceptual analysis for this project were made by the human team.

AI served as a tool that accelerated a large part of our work, particularly the computations. We used Claude Fable 5 and 5.1, Claude Opus 4.8, and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol for searching the literature, generating code, checking results, and proofreading. The workflow that eventually succeeded was a tightly controlled collaboration in which the computational work was much faster with AI, while the human collaborators continued to direct the research and verify the results. AI systems increased our confidence in tackling difficult problems and helped us communicate more efficiently across our different areas of expertise.”

I find this result fantastic (the paper is a gem by the way), and I think it exactly illustrates the way senior mathematicians (Lee, Poonen, Pries) can use LLMs to accelerate research and understanding, and include graduate students (Shaowu Zhang) and postdocs (Xiaoyu Huang) in the process!

Mathematics is never going to be the same and I recognize that the way I did research and found fulfillment from it are no longer here.

Mathematics will be different, yes, but I firmly believe it will be similar to what we do now, in all the best ways. As a final example, very recently three mathematicians (Elkies, Klagsbrun, and Li) have found an elliptic curve of rank 32. I find this discovery astonishing and wildly exciting. In a private communication, Zev Klagsbrun mentioned to me

“It would be a mistake to view this as a triumph of humans over AI. In fact, it’s a great example of humans using AI to push the boundary of what is known.”

I could not agree more. Immediately after their curve was found, my student Dylan Costa and I started working on finding a quadratic twist of their curve with rank bigger or equal to 3 (in order to find a quadratic field over which their curve achieves rank at least 35), and with the help of LLMs (in coding and literature search) we succeeded to find one, conditional to BSD/Parity. Both Dylan and I found the work on this little contribution (certainly little compared to the giant discovery of the rank 32 curve) to be exhilarating. It would not have been possible just a few months ago without the help of LLMs. This is why I would find it paradoxical to leave mathematics now.

I am not asking you to agree with my personal preferences.

I just want to conclude by thanking Anonymous for writing such a great piece that should make everyone in math think long and hard about the future of the profession. Thank you. And a final message just to Anonymous: I would love to record an interview with you and post it in my channel. Or send me an email message if you want to chat. Bye and best of luck!

Received 22 October 2026.

item.title: Disgusted by AI?
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: I completely disagree with the notion that AI companies have hijacked our mathematical culture and turned it into something new and unrecognizable. They have just taken our existing culture to its extreme.
item.content:encoded:
Marcus Zibrowius, Professor at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf

AI models are making mathematical progress at an unimaginable scale. There’s now a reasonable expectation that soon, we will be able to prove a theorem, or find a counterexample, at the touch of a button.

But the overall reaction of our mathematical community is closer to panic than it is to enthusiasm. AI is perceived as a threat, not just to humanity as a whole (which is a different story) but to mathematics specifically. We are collectively appalled by formally-verified but fully inexplicable proofs, and even more disgusted by companies that churn out one AI-generated (and equally verified) paper after the other without even having a single person on the team able to explain them.

We talk about the good old days when mathematics was about building a community of common understanding, facilitating personal growth, celebrating beauty.

What a feel-good fairy-tale that is!

In fact, our values have always been about who got there first. Collectively speaking, the one thing we, as a mathematical community, have always valued most has been a proof of a hitherto unproven theorem. It was not a nicer proof of a known result, and certainly not a beautiful exposition of a known proof.

You think I’m being cynical? Allow me to argue my point.

Follow the money.

Explaining a proof may have earned you an applause or a compliment. Completing a proof –\text{\textendash} and doing so faster than anyone else –\text{\textendash} is what has always had the potential of getting you a job. Also, when did you last write a grant proposal promising to deepen the communal understanding of an existing proof, or to find a more digestible proof to a proven theorem? How does the amount of funding you have acquired for promising new results compare to the funding you got for explaining existing ones?

Reflect on common behaviour.

What is more likely to keep you up at night? A fellow mathematician threatening to arrive at “your” result ahead of you, or a fellow mathematician having trouble understanding your arguments?

The other day, an eminent mathematician confessed to me over lunch that they worked through their summer holidays to get out a paper with a new construction that they got out of an AI model. Anyone asking the model the same question would get the same ingenious answer, so the logic went, hence they needed to publish this immediately.

On the flip side, I’ve sat through talks where the speaker afterwards, privately, declared “Today I have given a talk that was utterly incomprehensible. I’ve always wanted to give a talk like this.” To be fair, this was a singular, extreme case. But we would not tolerate this kind of behaviour if we really cared so much about a community of common understanding.

Acknowledge past grievances.

Personally, I vividly remember how, at a panel discussion on “Future Directions of Algebraic Topology” at Stanford in 2012, one of the younger members of the audience raised the question: What can we do to make mathematical culture more like music culture, where presenters are valued as much as composers? At that time, the idea of AI was still very much hypothetical. The question was about our very own, human culture.

Read the Leiden declaration.

The Leiden declaration, which has been widely endorsed by the mathematical community, lists the following as one of our five mathematical “values”:

Results are attributable to specific authors who take credit for their discovery and assume responsibility for their correctness. These principles ground the merit-based standards to which we aspire in mathematical research.

That is just another way of saying that the one thing that really matters for your standing within the community is that you arrive at a new result first.

So why am I saying this? Because I completely disagree with the notion that AI companies have hijacked our mathematical culture and turned it into something new and unrecognizable. They have not. Quite the opposite. They are playing to our rules. They are even solving our problems, problems that no one else cares about! They have just taken our existing culture to its extreme.

And now, we are disgusted!?

I would argue that what we’re really disgusted by is a key aspect of our own culture, now that we see it more clearly than ever before. We’re disgusted by the idea that getting there first is all that matters.

Let’s be honest about what was and what is. We defined our priorities. AI serves them better than we can. Perhaps, the priorities were off.

Received 25 September 2026.

item.title: Towards a world mathematical commons
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: Mathematics is changing and growing beyond us. Here's what we can do about it.
item.content:encoded:
Kunal Marwaha, Ph.D student at University of Chicago

SERIES · As application deadlines approach, Proofs and Prompts is publishing a series of posts from 19 to 23 October for people considering a PhD, doing a PhD or looking for a postdoc: guidelines, discussions and speculation about what to do and what careers in mathematics will look like. This post is one of them. Each is written independently and reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

Mathematics is a creative and emotional endeavor. We are driven by challenge and curiosity. We express our ideas carefully to be precisely understood. Our highest moments can fill us with exhilaration and awe.

But how we do mathematics has evolved over time. We have moved away from pictures and informal arguments; we now have axioms and proofs. We have outgrown the time when one person could have understood all of known mathematics; now, we specialize, relying on others to teach us what we know less about.

Today, it is clear that mathematics is again changing and growing beyond us. There exist machines which can prove new mathematical statements, and convert them into papers for humans to verify. This is strange and disruptive to our current process. However, I offer a positive vision of a future which includes these machines while preserving our motivations for this extreme passion.

We should change our mindset from explorers of the mathematical frontier to stewards of a world commons of mathematics.

A commons is a societal resource available to all because it improves everyone’s quality of life. My favorite example is the US National Park system. At a national park, I can reliably experience an overwhelm of natural beauty in mountains, forests, or rivers. I can camp, swim, or just walk on a trail. After a weekend trip, I return to my normal life refreshed and inspired.

I like the outdoors, but I am not very adventurous. For some people I know, the outdoors can feel like home. They will go into nature for weeks or months at a time: backpacking, rock climbing, journaling. One can make a living like this as a park ranger or firefighter; people in these jobs are paid to understand wildlife, take responsibility for keeping man and nature in balance, and build trails to make life pleasant for visitors like me.

We can build the same kind of environment for mathematics.

For many of us, research is more of a passion than a job. The mathematical outdoors feels like home. This is why theorem-proving machines can feel so intimidating: they are strange new creatures. I think the machines are here to stay, and I don’t think we can control which problems they will solve. Instead, we should learn from them, keep them in balance with human understanding, and show other humans the beauty of this place. We can be the rangers and firefighters of our mathematical parks, which are more alive than ever before.

The sudden advent of theorem-proving machines will make the next few years painful and difficult. However, if we do not act, we may quickly lose relevance, and our community is likely to wither. This makes building a mathematical commons extremely urgent. But what would it take to build this commons?

The most important step is to create a coalition of mathematicians to steward the commons. We should create a non-profit with a large advisory board, who represent the broad and diverse interests of people who prove or teach theorems in their work. This organization should not be run by any AI company, and our artifacts should be open to everyone.

The next step is to convert all mathematics into formally verified statements. This is the goal of the Mathematics Autoformalization Project. If we can use computer code to certify correctness of a proof, we can maintain our trust in these proofs at scale. Today, the most popular way to formally verify mathematics uses the Lean proof assistant. There is a vibrant open-source community around Mathlib, which has verified essentially all of undergraduate mathematics. It is now even possible to use LLMs to convert proofs of research-grade theorems directly into Lean. (The recent formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem used the public prove2.me site I helped build.)

Formalizing all of mathematics would create a large directed graph of known statements and their implications. Creating this graph is achievable if AI companies donate some compute resources to the mathematical commons. Here, they can work together instead of against each other. In the future, all new results could be added to this graph of knowledge.

The final step is to tame this graph of formally verified statements. We do not have to digest all at once; we only have to manage it. We should cluster and sparsify the graph until it corresponds to human-sized chunks of knowledge. We can look for simplifications, common definitions, and unifying theories. We can build trails through wonderful proofs to share both with other mathematicians and with “park visitors”. This can all be assisted by machines, provided it helps accomplish our goals.

If done well, the commons will bring about a golden age for human understanding. With responsible stewardship, we can nurture the next generation of mathematicians and math appreciators alongside theorem-proving machines.

Let us start by building this broad coalition of mathematicians. If we work together, we can steer the way mathematics evolves in this uncertain future.

Kunal Marwaha

Received 5 October 2026, revised 23 October 2026.

item.title: The Rules Cannot Change Only for Young Mathematicians: AI and the future of a mathematical career
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “I am writing neither to defend a complete ban on AI nor to celebrate its unrestricted use, but because I no longer know what rules I am expected to follow, what work will count as my own, or how today's decisions will affect my career. […]”
item.content:encoded:
Anonymous, Postdoc

SERIES · As application deadlines approach, Proofs and Prompts is publishing a series of posts from 19 to 23 October for people considering a PhD, doing a PhD or looking for a postdoc: guidelines, discussions and speculation about what to do and what careers in mathematics will look like. This post is one of them. Each is written independently and reflects only its authors’ views. All posts in the series

AI assistance disclosure: AI was used to translate my draft into English, revise its language and organization, assist with literature searches, and suggest relevant quotations and statistics. The personal experiences and central concerns originate in my draft.

I am a postdoctoral mathematician working in partial differential equations, and I love what I do. I have preferred doing mathematics to expressing opinions in public, but the rapid changes of recent months have made that difficult.

I am writing neither to defend a complete ban on AI nor to celebrate its unrestricted use, but because I no longer know what rules I am expected to follow, what work will count as my own, or how today’s decisions will affect my career.

For an established professor, uncertainty about the future may be a subject for an interesting essay; for a doctoral student or postdoc, it can determine whether years of work lead to a job. The same advice does not carry the same risk for everyone.

My concern is not only what AI can do to mathematics, but what mathematicians and institutions are choosing to do to one another during this transition.

1. We are told that priority will matter less, but the race suggests otherwise

A recurring message in the recent debate is that recognition should move from being first toward understanding proofs, explaining their ideas, and making them useful to others.

In Mathematics in the age of AI, Terence Tao argues for less emphasis on proof generation and being first. Amit Harlev goes further: “when a result is proven by an AI, priority should carry no reward.” Timothy Gowers predicts that the credit system will collapse, while defending credit as long as careers depend on it. Benoit Henry questions whether a theorem belongs to whoever obtains it first when someone else could quickly do so with a similar system. [1, 2, 3, 4]

Bryna Kra offers a concrete proposal: “Journals need to distinguish and credit the roles of discovery, proof, formalization and explanation.” Grant Sanderson observes that “every AI-generated proof is born an unsolved exposition problem.” [5, 6]

I welcome greater credit for explanation, but cannot behave as though that transition has happened while the consequences of being second remain uncertain. A postdoc cannot pay rent with a prediction that exposition will eventually become prestigious.

The possibility that another person or laboratory could obtain a proof quickly can intensify the pressure to announce first, even as we are asked to slow down, check the literature, understand everything, and write carefully.

Nor do I accept that mathematics was always about understanding rather than solving problems: I value both learning a beautiful argument and finding one that did not previously exist. I do not want either experience dismissed merely because the other may be easier to preserve.

The familiar name “Fermat’s little theorem” reminds me that discovery, proof, and naming are not the same thing. Historical names offer no reliable rulebook for present-day authorship; we need to distinguish priority, authorship, attribution, and understanding explicitly.

2. What exactly does an AI-generated proof entitle its producer to claim?

Jihao Liu states the practical dilemma unusually clearly:

“Consider the following situation. I use AI to produce a paper whose result is important. What should I do?

  1. I post the paper to arXiv. Then I am criticized for not having verified the paper in detail. This goes against my values as a mathematician.
  2. I do not post the paper anywhere. But what if someone else obtains the result and posts it before me? In that case I lose the credit.” [7]

He posts some machine-checked, not yet human-verified papers on a separate webpage rather than arXiv, and requires a timestamp when recognizing prior independent work. [7]

Liu is frank about protecting priority, but the order troubles me: secure the claim first, complete verification and repair attribution afterward. Treating credit as his to grant strikes me as cynical. His offers of shared credit and coauthorship recognize the value of checking, simplifying, and explaining, but leave unclear what the announcement reserves and what later contributors can earn. [7]

What credit has the initial producer earned before these other contributions have been made? Does a public timestamp establish priority for a theorem, a candidate argument, or merely a generated document? If the proof is correct but its attribution incomplete, what is owed to the people whose ideas supplied most of it?

Marco Trombetti’s ProofForum proposal distinguishes generating, checking, repairing, simplifying, and explaining without endorsing Liu’s entire policy: “verification could itself become a visible mathematical contribution.” Recognition need not stop with the generator, and credibility can develop through public examination. [8] That may be useful, but a record of contributions is not yet an agreed system for allocating jobs, prizes, publishing rights, or theorem names.

Ruodu Wang supports human understanding and rewriting, but identifies the incentive problem: “Being the second to solve a problem has low or no value.” His model rewards posting AI output immediately over taking time to understand and rewrite it. [9] Even a reduced but positive reward for first place preserves that disadvantage if second place earns nothing; Wang’s argument is that careful work needs changed incentives, not advice alone. [9]

Removing priority creates another difficulty: junior researchers depend on the problems they solve, rather than the established reputations and other recognized roles of senior mathematicians. Wang writes: “I do not see a good system of evaluating junior mathematicians.” A new ideal is not yet a viable career. [9]

We cannot preserve the reward for speed, demand slow and careful work, and leave the people with the least job security to absorb the conflict.

3. The Navier–Stokes dispute: different results, unresolved standards

The September controversy involving Tristan Buckmaster, Levent Alpöge, and OpenAI left me with a bitter feeling. As a PDE researcher, I wanted to understand both the mathematics and its implications for research practice.

The mathematical claims should first be kept distinct. OpenAI’s September 8 announcement claimed a smooth-forcing Navier–Stokes blow-up result establishing alternatives C and D of the Millennium Prize formulation, alongside a separate unforced Euler result. It distinguishes these from Alpöge and Buckmaster’s forced Euler work and denies that their unpublished work or recent Codex prompts influenced its system. These are OpenAI’s stated claims and account. [10]

In the Q&A of Buckmaster’s September 23rd NYU talk, he says: “Those physical mechanisms that I can explain to you guys came out from LLM.” In his account, AI supplied important mechanisms while human expertise directed the search and helped reconstruct the argument. A label such as “Alpöge–Buckmaster, 2026” therefore needs a clear account of what the researchers proposed, what the systems generated, and who verified and rewrote the proof. [12]

He also describes working with Alpöge through internal models: “it’s not just internal models it’s internal compute.” His point that many agents can matter as much as a better model distinguishes their resources from an ordinary subscription. [12]

Buckmaster questions credit based on “who does something the fastest” and says: “I think this race dynamics doesn’t make sense.” WIRED reports that he released unfinished papers to get ahead of OpenAI’s announcement and accepted responsibility for cleaning them up. Wanting priority to matter less while protecting work under unchanged rules is understandable—and precisely the dilemma younger mathematicians face. The question is not whether one researcher should have solved the incentive problem alone, but whether the community can advise young mathematicians to leave the race while continuing to reward those who enter it. [12, 11]

As of 1 October, more than three weeks after the 7 September announcement, I had not found a revised exposition of the forced Euler proof that resolved my readability concerns. Expecting a world-class fluid dynamics expert such as Buckmaster to produce one does not settle what recognition the initial release deserves. [27]

If an unfinished announcement preserves recognition while a readable proof follows later, is the same option open to a doctoral student or postdoc? What standard of verification and exposition must be met before release, and what recognition remains available to someone who waits?

Buckmaster’s talk and NYU’s announcement explicitly credit Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa’s program and strategy, yet public attention can favor the final announcement over the work that made it possible. [12, 27]

Neither Isabella Ward’s 19 September WIRED article, “Mathematicians Feel Threatened by AI. They Can’t Quit It,” nor the 8 September OfficeChai report, “OpenAI Says It Didn’t See Any Of Buckmaster And Alpöge’s Work While Resolving Navier-Stokes,” names Córdoba or Martínez-Zoroa. My concern is that press coverage of priority disputes in the AI era will tend to focus on who obtained or announced a result first, while overlooking the foundational mathematical work—and the people behind it—that made those AI-assisted discoveries possible. [11, 28]

4. This is not an abstract problem for me

I have checked and rewritten an AI-generated proof of a problem I had not worked on for roughly ten years, but have not published it. A group I will not name is pursuing the same question; as far as I know, they have not resolved it, and my argument appears to take a different route from their earlier attempts. Should I post it with a detailed account of the AI contribution, contact the group first, or offer collaboration? If I present the result at a conference, should I write “Theorem [my name, 2026]” on the slide, and would publishing it help my career, damage my reputation, or both?

I am not asking to claim someone else’s ideas, but what credit checking and rewriting earns; that cannot depend on which influential mathematician is asked.

Meanwhile, I am finishing a substantial article developed over about a year with pen and paper, not with AI. Almost daily, I fear being scooped by someone, perhaps using AI, who posts first: my understanding would remain, but the publication opportunity and recognition for a year of independent work might not.

Antonio Auffinger’s Open problems, open mathematics warns that others can quickly complete a publicly shared strategy, making unfinished ideas risky to share. His call to reshape incentives aims to protect openness for the least secure researchers. [13] I want to continue sharing ideas, asking colleagues questions, and doing careful work without making secrecy, haste, and suspicion the rational way to survive.

5. Recognition, jobs, and the cost of disclosure

Another part of the debate makes these choices even more difficult: some mathematicians do not merely question the value of AI-generated papers, but predict reputational damage for AI users or propose institutional preferences against their work.

In Where I Stand on AI, Vladimir Lazić predicts that attaching one’s name to a partially AI-produced paper can destroy a mathematician’s reputation. Addressing researchers without tenure, he writes:

“you will never get tenure, unless you are being pushed by someone in your camp who has tenure.” [14]

Although this is a prediction rather than evidence about hiring committees generally, a junior researcher cannot ignore the possibility that some evaluators share that attitude.

Donatella Iacono, explicitly following Lazić’s principles, states: “I do not support hiring of academic staff who use AI as a substitute for their own work.” She takes the same position on supervising doctoral and postdoctoral researchers. [32]

Max Weinreich goes beyond predicting reputational consequences: in The crisis of AI-generated mathematics, he proposes “reserving hire lines for mathematicians who eschew AI” and “valuing AI-free papers more highly in tenure promotion.” These are proposals for allocating opportunities differently, not merely expressions of a personal preference. [15]

Atticus Stonestrom makes a direct proposal about access to publication:

“Traditional journals should ban papers in which AI has played a coauthor-level role, and new venues should be established for the publication of such papers.” [16]

Without a ban, Stonestrom proposes distinguishing such papers and capping their annual publication. He cites authorship and scarce refereeing resources, acknowledges that restrictions may encourage concealment, but argues that this should not determine standards. Even a carefully checked paper could be excluded from a traditional journal. [16]

A young researcher does not need a profession-wide ban to find these positions alarming: a few editors or hiring-committee members can have a decisive effect on a career. Honest disclosure may carry lasting consequences when it can reduce recognition or make a paper ineligible for a journal.

Martin Hairer instead argues that “articles are judged on their merits, independently of the tools being used” and that disclosure should not automatically reduce a paper’s value, while retaining human scrutiny, understanding, and writing as requirements. [17]

What should a postdoc make of these competing messages: use AI responsibly and disclose it, avoid it to demonstrate independent ability, use it or fall behind, yet risk losing recognition by doing so? These are not small differences in taste when employment is at stake.

I have heard colleagues describe the strongest anti-AI views as resistance to an inevitable technology, while others say they reflect a larger, quieter part of the profession. I do not know which claim is correct, since neither a collection of essays nor my conversations establishes what most mathematicians believe.

What is already visible is uncertainty about the consequences of honesty, and that uncertainty deserves an institutional response.

6. What the publication and disclosure data actually show

The data show rapid change without establishing how much AI use is undisclosed or why.

Tammy Kolda and Daniel Appelo count 6,307 primary-mathematics arXiv announcements in August 2026, up 2,785 from 3,522 a year earlier—about 79%, versus 43% across arXiv. [18]

Benoit Henry reports single-author counts of 1,174 and 2,603 for those months (about 122% growth), with 809 later papers mentioning AI. He cautions that the counts are uncertain; single authorship is not evidence of AI use, and an AI mention is not necessarily a carefully classified disclosure. [4]

Xiaoshn Nee, Haobo Zhong, and Xiaomin Ni find growth in 29 of 30 primary mathematics categories; the share of active author units posting at least five papers in January–August rose from 2.45% in 2025 to 3.80% in 2026. [29]

Tara Abrishami’s Epoch AI analysis finds that disclosures of any AI use rose from 3.89% in April 2026 to 25.25% in August (1,453 of 5,754 papers); 337, or 5.86%, disclosed substantial research contributions. The broader category includes writing, computation, and literature review. [19]

Yet three quarters of Epoch’s August papers made no acknowledgment; this group grew from 3,260 in August 2025 to 4,301 in August 2026 (about 32%). Silence does not tell us whether AI was used, and differing corpora and counting conventions prevent simply combining the studies’ totals. [19]

In Kimball Martin’s August 2026 number-theory sample, 12.0% disclosed AI writing while 20.7% were flagged for apparent AI writing. The imperfect detector and unpublished scoring rule make this suggestive only; Martin warns that a score is not a verdict. [20]

These counts neither identify concealed use in individual papers nor prove large-scale concealment, but common sense suggests that incentives to publish faster, coupled with fear of penalties for disclosure, can encourage silence. I suspect some use goes unacknowledged partly because of stigma.

Harlev identifies the underlying incentive: evaluating declared AI work less favorably can punish honest researchers without reliably detecting undisclosed use. [2] We should therefore demand precise disclosures and fair evaluation together, since one without the other creates a predictable conflict.

7. Equal rules require more than equal advice

Access depends not only on whether someone chooses to use AI, but on the models, computing budget, and support available to them. OpenAI’s September account describes an internal model more capable than the public comparator, placing that work in a different setting from a postdoc’s ordinary subscription. [10]

I worry that personal connections to laboratories may become a research advantage. Does staying competitive now require knowing someone who can provide access to an internal system or a large computing budget? What happens to mathematicians who have neither those connections nor an institution able to buy equivalent resources? Such access must be visible in evaluation: a publication list should not conceal the difference between an individual subscription and large, privately supported searches.

The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence’s September 29 recommendations warn that proprietary models risk a “two-tier system” and unequal access to public models a “multi-tier hierarchy.” It calls for broad, equitable access. [21]

On 1 October 2026, Claude Max 20x and ChatGPT Pro 200 each cost US$200 monthly; the new ChatGPT Pro 500 costs US$500. Both highest-tier subscriptions total US$700 monthly, or US$8,400 annually, before taxes, exchange charges, and separate computing costs. [30, 31]

Across developing countries and lower-paid academic systems in developed countries, stipends and salaries may leave little for these subscriptions after living expenses, especially when researchers personally fund multiple services. An expense routine for a well-funded department may be unsustainable for an equally capable mathematician elsewhere, rewarding institutional resources and personal finances rather than talent, effort, or the quality of research questions.

Researchers should not have to choose between living expenses and tools increasingly treated as necessary. Institutional support helps, but identical prices do not mean equal access, and subscriptions do not fund thousands of parallel agents.

The Leiden Declaration links AI use to human responsibility, transparency, and its effects on the profession; these principles must apply equally to researchers with and without privileged access. [22]

Orwell’s Animal Farm comes to mind when formal equality coexists with unequal opportunities: I do not want one standard for insiders and another for outsiders, or strict rules for students with exceptions for established names.

8. What future are we offering PhD students?

I welcome the Harvard summit on doctoral education in the age of AI. Its September 17–18 meeting brought together 24 mathematicians, produced recommendations for departmental discussion, and explicitly thanked the graduate students and postdocs who participated in a panel. [23]

Consultation, however, is not the same as an ongoing role in decisions. How will students and postdocs participate in setting the rules that govern their training and evaluation? Who will represent people outside the institutions already most influential in this debate?

The report favors demonstrated mastery over the dissertation alone and says it “need not be a requirement for the thesis to have recorded the first proof.” This may protect students whose work is unexpectedly overtaken, but protection within a PhD program does not automatically carry into the job market. [24]

If an adviser asks a student to wait until an AI-generated argument is fully understood, and someone else posts a less readable version first, will the student still receive comparable recognition? Will thesis and hiring committees use compatible standards?

There can be good educational reasons to restrict tools while students learn a skill; equal treatment need not mean identical training for students and experienced researchers, but the distinction must be explained, bounded, and accompanied by protection against resulting disadvantages.

Senior mathematicians should ask what research opportunities they are preserving for students. If a problem can now be explored quickly using AI, should every such opportunity become another paper on an established researcher’s list, or could some become genuinely collaborative training projects? This concerns mentorship when the supply of attractive projects may change rapidly, not a demand that senior researchers stop research.

Above all, what life are we inviting a talented mathematics graduate to pursue? Many of us entered the subject because we wanted to experience the struggle and joy of discovery: working through failed ideas, finding the right argument, and reaching a moment of understanding through our own effort.

Jonny Evans explains why research produces more than a paper: “The ‘output’ is a person who understands something better,” someone who can carry that understanding into research and teaching. I share his concern that more results do not necessarily mean more capable mathematicians. [33]

Teaching, exposition, and verification are already part of the mathematics I love, but a career centered on checking machine output, teaching calculus, linear algebra, and differential equations to engineering and computer-science students, and explaining results generated inside commercial laboratories may not appeal to people who hoped to become researchers. Calling that concern nostalgia does not answer it.

I fear losing both discovery and professional security while being told that a more demanding system of oral assessments and repeated demonstrations of understanding is the solution. Such assessments may be appropriate, but they do not, by themselves, offer a positive account of the career that follows.

A field that fails to attract and support its next generation cannot preserve itself through inspiring statements alone.

9. What institutions need to say clearly

What I need from the people who hire, promote, edit journals, award grants, and supervise students is not another assurance that mathematics will always matter, but practical answers.

Ben Antieau puts one proposal plainly: “Do not recruit, hire, promote, or praise based on the number of papers.” Daniel Litt argues that sustained mathematical discussion and talks can demonstrate understanding better than papers alone. Henry similarly asks hiring committees to stop counting articles. [25, 26, 4]

These proposals need to become public rules before researchers can rely on them when choosing projects, tools, or publication venues.

I want clear answers in six areas.

Permitted use and responsibility. Which uses of AI are acceptable in research, dissertations, and submitted papers? How do the rules distinguish language editing, coding, literature searches, suggested lemmas, generated proofs, and largely autonomous work? What must every named author understand and be able to defend?

Release and priority. May someone release a proof that is not human-verified? Does a Lean-checked proof have a different status? Is understanding the broad strategy sufficient, or must the details be checked before release? What priority, if any, attaches to an unfinished write-up accompanied by a promise to improve it?

Authorship and attribution. What contributions justify authorship, and what contributions require a different form of recognition? How are the people who supplied prior methods, directed the search, repaired the proof, formalized it, or explained it credited? What must happen when the initial attribution is incomplete?

Hiring, promotion, and publication. Will good, selective mathematics journals accept AI-generated but human-verified proofs under the same standards as other research papers? How much original human input will they require? Will a clear explanation, simplification, or independent reconstruction of an already announced AI result satisfy their standards of originality and significance, or be excluded as exposition? Will those requirements be public before authors invest months in a project?

Will hiring and promotion committees continue to expect the same quantity of publications, journal prestige, citation counts, and h-index as before—or raise those expectations because AI can accelerate production? If understanding and exposition are to count more, what evidence will be accepted in place of those measures, and will it lead to comparable professional opportunities? Will a mathematician working without AI be judged against AI-assisted output rates? Will someone who discloses careful AI use be penalized for doing so? How can candidates challenge decisions based on standards that were never announced?

Training and protection. How will students retain opportunities for independent discovery? How will a student who follows careful verification rules be protected from the resulting delay? How will institutions recognize substantial work that loses chronological priority?

Access and implementation. Who will fund the tools that new expectations require? How will unequal model access and computing budgets be considered? Which rules apply across institutions, when do they begin, and how will students and postdocs participate in reviewing them?

I am asking not for a universal numerical formula for mathematical worth, but for public standards that guide decisions without changing according to a person’s reputation.

10. The future should not be decided over our heads

For the first time, I am seriously considering leaving mathematics—a painful sentence to write after almost twenty-five years of passion, thought, and effort. What makes me consider leaving is not that a machine can do something I cannot, but that I no longer trust the profession to offer a fair and intelligible path forward.

What troubles me most is the possibility that established researchers will keep the advantages of the old system while younger people accept the obligations of a new one. Even when individuals act in good faith, the appearance of that double standard is damaging and should be addressed through transparent rules rather than dismissed as anxiety about technological change.

What I am asking for is a profession in which careful work is not punished for being slow, honesty is not punished for being visible, and access to powerful tools is not confused with mathematical merit.

I would welcome an emergency international meeting, with the reach and seriousness of an ICM, devoted to these questions. It should include doctoral students, postdocs, mathematicians from less wealthy institutions and countries, journal editors, hiring committees, and funding bodies—not only the people who already have the most secure positions. Its aim should be concrete, revisable standards for research, credit, training, and careers, together with a timetable for putting them into practice.

No meeting can settle every question permanently, but we can do better than leaving young researchers to discover the real rules only when an application is rejected.

My deepest fear is not that AI will destroy the career of a mathematician, but that mathematicians will make it unlivable through unequal rules, opaque incentives, and a failure to protect the people who come next.

I do not yet have a settled position on every use of AI in mathematics, but I do have a clear position on fairness: the rules cannot change only for the young.
